distillation_scope.manifold_definition: Localized necrotizing infection of lung parenchyma forming a pus-filled cavity, usually with surrounding pneumonia and often an air-fluid level when the cavity communicates with an airway.
distillation_scope.disease_name_scope: Disease prompt medical input is only Lung abscess. Etiology, source, chronicity, microbiology, severity, drainage need, and mimic context are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk factors, treatment modifiers, or event hazards rather than disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Aspiration of oral anaerobes, microaerophilic streptococci, mixed upper-airway flora, or infected secretions into dependent or obstructed lung segments.
Mixed anaerobic, facultative, microaerophilic streptococcal, staphylococcal, gram-negative, mycobacterial, fungal, or secondary-source infection expands within consolidated lung parenchyma.
Neutrophil-rich proteolysis, tissue ischemia, bacterial toxins, and impaired clearance liquefy infected lung, creating a thick-walled pus cavity.
Communication between the abscess cavity and bronchial tree permits air entry, air-fluid level formation, cough, copious or putrid sputum, and potential aspiration of abscess contents.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Secondary obstruction or non-aspiration source pressure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endobronchial tumor, foreign body, bronchiectasis, infected infarct, septic embolus, contiguous subdiaphragmatic infection, or structural lung disease can create or maintain an abscess and increase nonresolution risk.
Peripheral abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or rupture can extend across visceral pleura, causing complicated parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bronchopleural fistula, or chest-wall extension.
Local necrotizing infection can drive fever, acute-phase response, leukocytosis, bacteremia, hypotension, lactate rise, AKI, and septic shock.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Gas-exchange failure from consolidation, cavity burden, or spillover
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Surrounding pneumonia, shunt, airway pus burden, atelectasis, empyema, and aspiration of abscess contents impair oxygenation and can require ventilatory support.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Large cavities are less likely to clear rapidly with antibiotics alone.
Airway communication can produce both an air-fluid level and sputum drainage.
Lower saturation raises respiratory failure risk.
Escalating support is a near-term marker of ventilator risk.
Pleural fluid adjacent to abscess can become infected or loculated.
Uncontrolled pleural infection increases death risk.

Pleural drainage or decortication when empyema is present

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Poor dentition raises oral anaerobic and Streptococcus anginosus group burden.
Anaerobic oral flora increases foul sputum probability.
Oral anaerobic burden makes anaerobic coverage more important.
Loss of airway protection or aspiration events seed dependent lung.
Aspiration often produces surrounding pneumonic infiltrate.
Impaired host response may slow closure.
Structural lung disease impairs clearance and creates local nidus.
Cancer can obstruct bronchi or mimic abscess; immunosuppression broadens pathogen spectrum.
Immunosuppression can blunt leukocytosis or permit severe infection.
Obstruction is a secondary abscess substrate and nonresolution driver.
Obstruction must be removed or sampled to clear the abscess.
Hematogenous seeding can create cavitary pulmonary lesions but often belongs to septic emboli/endocarditis manifold when present.
Multiple peripheral cavitary lesions may be embolic rather than primary abscess.
Large or persistent cavity increases drainage/source-control need.
Imaging must determine whether minimally invasive drainage is feasible.

supportive_care: Do not split first-layer Lung abscess by aspiration, organism, acute/chronic course, community/hospital setting, abscess size, or severity.

Presentation ranking should use early symptoms, exam, vitals, labs, and presentation imaging. Culture, bronchoscopy, pathology, cytology, drainage findings, and treatment response are confirmatory unless known at presentation.

Actively evaluate near-neighbor mimics: pneumonia without abscess, pleural empyema, TB/NTM, cavitating cancer, septic pulmonary emboli/endocarditis, pulmonary infarct/cavitation, fungal disease, and vasculitis.

CT should assess cavity location, wall, air-fluid level, size, surrounding consolidation, tree-in-bud pattern, pleural effusion/empyema, multiplicity, vascular proximity, bronchial obstruction, and possible tumor or foreign body.
Microbiology should be sought before antibiotics when feasible, but negative cultures do not exclude lung abscess because anaerobes and prior antibiotics reduce yield.

Antibiotic selection should be modulated by active coverage, anaerobic coverage, local resistance, aspiration/oral source context, immune status, allergy, renal function, and culture/susceptibility when available.

Drainage/source control becomes more important for large cavities, persistent fever or leukocytosis, poor antibiotic response, thick or loculated collections, pleural extension, respiratory compromise, or suspected obstruction.
Pleural effusion next to an abscess needs empyema assessment; pleural drainage/decortication is a separate source-control vector when pleural infection dominates.

Support oxygenation, airway clearance, nutrition, glycemic control, dental/oral source control, aspiration prevention, and rehabilitation while monitoring for hemoptysis, bronchopleural fistula, empyema, sepsis, AKI, and respiratory failure.
